Bill Gates Jeffrey Epstein — EFTA02730265, the 2013 "Points" memo.

When Gates's science adviser Boris Nikolic left bgC3, Gates's lawyer Larry Cohen sent the draft separation terms to Jeffrey Epstein: "Wanted to get these to you for input." The terms: mutual non-disparagement, no legal claims against Gates, his family, the foundation, or bgC3 — ever. Signed: Bill Gates. Nikolic's own edit the next morning: move the date, and rewrite the point about Epstein "helping me find a job."

2,620 documents in the DOJ releases name Bill Gates. This one is his office's paperwork inside Epstein's inbox.

Elon Musk Jeffrey Epstein email — EFTA02338119, December 2013.

Musk, from his own account, Dec 13, 2013: "Will be in the BVI/St Bart's area over the holidays. Is there a good time to visit?" Epstein: "Anytime. I will be there 28–7th." Musk, next day: "Is there a day/night that you would particularly recommend within those dates?"

The email does not show whether the visit happened. Musk has said publicly that he declined to visit Epstein's island. The archive publishes the document — and the limit of what it proves.

Mark Zuckerberg Epstein files — 385 mentions. Contact: zero.

No email, no meeting, no call: across the DOJ releases, the Barak leak, and House Oversight, no document shows Zuckerberg communicating with Epstein. The mentions are other people's paper — a 2019 donation pitch to Epstein citing Zuckerberg's $3 million Breakthrough Awards as the model (EFTA00034221), and a Davos conference pitch name-checking him (EFTA02262778).

Gates has paperwork. Musk has an email. Zuckerberg has mentions. A name in the files is not a relationship — and the archive publishes the difference.
